subject: English
source: Tarbiyyah Primary English scheme of work for Frozen Kingdom (the school's own adaptation of the Cornerstones English unit), with the founding-year bridge (grammar essentials, retrieval and inference, formal letter); The Call of the Wild (Jack London) opening paraphrased; creative writing frameworks (STASS, HOOK, TCCC), VIPERS reading, reading journal and English intervention booklets; National Curriculum Year 6 English.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Grammar, punctuation and vocabulary (SATs skills)
lessons.title: Word classes and the GPS paper
objectives: Name the main word classes and spot them in sentences
Understand the layout and question types of the KS2 GPS test

keywords.def: the group a word belongs to, such as noun, verb or adverb
a word that introduces a noun, such as the, a, my, some
a word such as because or although that joins a clause to a main clause
a word or phrase that adds information about a verb

starter: Say bismillah. Underline the verb: The children walked to the mosque.
Write a sentence with a relative clause.
Correct: We was happy and them books were lost.

teach.heading: Why GPS matters
bullets: Paper 1: grammar and punctuation, about 45 minutes
Skills help your reading and writing too
teach.note: Begin with bismillah and explain the plan for the half term. The SATs are taken in May; today we start the skills we need. Reassure pupils: the test measures what we have learnt, and regular practice will help. Show the question types: tick, circle, underline, rewrite, insert punctuation.

teach.heading: Eight word classes
teach.note: Run a quick-fire on mini-whiteboards. Give example words and ask for the class. Misconception: pupils think each word always has one class. Show 'run' as a verb ('I run') and a noun ('a morning run').

teach.heading: Clues to word class
bullets: Nouns follow the, a or my
Adverbs often tell how, when or where
teach.note: Teach tests: Can I put 'the' before it? Can I change its tense? Show the sentence 'The tall boy ran quickly across the field' and label each word.

teach.heading: Phrases and clauses
bullets: A phrase has no verb and subject
A clause has a subject and a verb
A main clause makes sense alone
teach.note: Give examples: 'in the garden' (phrase), 'the boy ran' (clause), 'because he was late' (subordinate clause). Explain subordinate clauses depend on a main clause.

teach.heading: Test strategies
bullets: Check how many answers you need
Check by reading the sentence aloud
teach.note: Practise a sample question: 'Circle the adverb in this sentence.' Teach how to work out marks from the number of answers needed.

practice: Label the word classes: The old man walked slowly home.
Is 'because he was late' a main clause or subordinate clause?
Circle the preposition: The cat slept under the table.
independent: Complete a ten-question word class quiz.
Underline the subordinate clause in six sentences.
Write two sentences using the word 'run' as a verb and a noun.
exit: Name the word class of 'quickly' in: She walked quickly.
What is a determiner? Give one.
lessons.homework: Write ten sentences using different word classes and label each one.
lessons.send: SEND: use colour coding for word classes. EAL: build a word class glossary with pictures. Stretch: find words that belong to more than one class and write sentences for each.

lessons.title: Bridge grammar: active and passive voice
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do reports use the passive voice?
objectives: To use the passive voice to change the focus of a sentence and create a formal tone
successCriteria: All: identify active and passive sentences
Most: change active sentences to passive
Some: explain when the passive is the better choice
lessons.crossCurricular: History: reporting the Titanic disaster
lessons.smsc: Moral: being careful with blame when facts are not yet known

keywords.def: the subject does the action: The ship hit the iceberg.
the subject has the action done to it: The iceberg was hit.
who or what does the action in a passive sentence (by the ship)
serious language for official writing

hook.text: "Someone left the lifeboats half empty." versus "The lifeboats were launched half empty." Which would an official report use? Why?
hook.a: The passive: it focuses on what happened, sounds formal and does not blame without evidence.

resources: Display: active and passive diagram
Punctuation Intervention Booklet (Lesson 1: Capital letters and end marks) for pupils who need extra support
Mini-whiteboard and pen
Exercise book

starter.q: Find the verb: The lookout spotted the iceberg.
Who did the action in that sentence?

model.problem: The lookout spotted the iceberg.
steps: Object becomes subject: The iceberg
Add was or were plus the past participle: was spotted
Optional agent: by the lookout
Result: The iceberg was spotted by the lookout.
model.answer: The iceberg was spotted by the lookout.

teach.heading: Why use the passive?
bullets: Focus on the event or object
teach.note: Examples: Warnings were received. The ship was built in Belfast.

check.q: Which sentence is passive?
check.why: In B the lifeboats receive the action (were lowered).

practice.q: Make passive: Engineers designed the hull.
practice.a: The hull was designed by engineers.
practice.model: Teacher works this one aloud: read the question, underline the key words, link it to today's rule, then give the answer in a full sentence: The hull was designed by engineers.

practice.q: Make active: The message was sent by the radio operator.
practice.a: The radio operator sent the message.

independent.q: Core: change eight active sentences about the Titanic into the passive (in the portal response box, with the sentence starter and paragraph frame)
independent.model: Teacher does the first part aloud before pupils start, showing each step: Eight correct passives

independent.q: Extend: write a formal paragraph about a ship's launch using three passives
Stretch: explain when an active sentence would be better
independent.a: For example: in a story, to show who acted and add drama

exit.q: Make passive: The storm damaged the rail.
exit.a: The rail was damaged by the storm.

lessons.homework: Find two passive sentences in a news article or information book. Read for 20 minutes a day.
lessons.send: SEND: colour-coded sentence parts to rearrange. EAL: was/were + past participle table. Stretch: use the passive with a modal (It should have been noticed).

lessons.title: Bridge grammar: formal register and the subjunctive
lessons.bigQuestion: How do I make my writing sound formal enough for an official reader?
objectives: To use formal vocabulary, structures and the subjunctive in formal writing
successCriteria: All: replace informal words with formal ones
Most: use formal structures (passive, no contractions, precise vocabulary)
Some: use the subjunctive correctly (If I were..., It is essential that he be...)
lessons.crossCurricular: Citizenship: official inquiries and reports
lessons.smsc: Social: respectful, precise language when addressing authorities

keywords.def: how formal or informal language is
a verb form for wishes, demands or unreal situations: If I were...
precise, serious words, like request instead of ask
a shortened form like don't

hook.text: "If I was captain, I'd have slowed down." Now say it as an official inquiry would. What changes?
hook.a: "Were the captain to have reduced speed..." or "If I were the captain, I would have reduced speed." (subjunctive, no contraction, formal verb)

pictures.find: official report document with seal photograph

pictures.alt: a ship's wheel on the bridge

resources: Vocabulary Intervention Programme (Lesson 20: Formal and informal vocabulary) for pupils who need extra support
Formal vocabulary word mat (ask → request, get → obtain, enough → sufficient)
Mini-whiteboard and pen
Exercise book

starter.q: Make passive: Officials questioned the crew.
starter.a: The crew were questioned by officials.

model.problem: Subjunctive forms
steps: Unreal situation: If I were the captain, I would slow down.
Demand: The inquiry insists that every ship carry enough lifeboats.
Formal wish: I wish it were possible to undo the disaster.
Note: were for all persons; base verb (carry, be) after demands
model.answer: Three correct subjunctive sentences.

misconception.wrong: If he was more careful, it would not have happened.
misconception.right: If he were more careful... (or: Had he been more careful, it would not have happened.)

check.q: Which uses the subjunctive?
options: If I was you, I would stay.
If I were you, I would stay.
If I am you, I stay.
check.why: were is the subjunctive form for an unreal situation.

practice.q: Make formal: We need to find out what went wrong.
practice.a: It is necessary to establish what went wrong.
practice.model: Teacher works this one aloud: read the question, underline the key words, link it to today's rule, then give the answer in a full sentence: It is necessary to establish what went wrong.

practice.q: Use the subjunctive: The law demands that each ship (have) lifeboats.
practice.a: The law demands that each ship have lifeboats.

independent.q: Core: rewrite a 6-sentence informal message about the Titanic as a formal statement (in the portal response box, with the sentence starter and paragraph frame)
independent.model: Labelled model to go through first (Subjunctive forms): Unreal situation: If I were the captain, I would slow down. | Demand: The inquiry insists that every ship carry enough lifeboats. | Formal wish: I wish it were possible to undo the disaster. | Note: were for all persons; base verb (carry, be) after demands | Result: Three correct subjunctive sentences.

independent.q: Extend: write three subjunctive sentences about safety at sea
Stretch: explain how the subjunctive changes the tone
independent.a: It sounds more formal and hypothetical

exit.q: Correct for formal writing: If she was older, she could go.
exit.a: If she were older, she could go.

lessons.homework: Rewrite three sentences from a text message as formal sentences. Read for 20 minutes a day.
lessons.send: SEND: word mat with matching pairs. EAL: subjunctive pattern card. Stretch: use "Were..." inversion (Were the warnings heeded, ...).

lessons.title: Colons and semi-colons for effect in thriller writing
lessons.bigQuestion: How can one punctuation mark change the rhythm of a sentence?
objectives: To understand how colons and semi-colons link ideas and create effects
successCriteria: All: use a colon to introduce a list or a reveal
Most: use a semi-colon to join two closely related main clauses
Some: use both in a thriller paragraph for effect

keywords.def: a mark (:) that introduces a list, an explanation or a reveal
a mark (;) that joins two related main clauses
a clause that makes sense on its own
a surprise that is shown to the reader

hook.text: "Only one thing was missing: the key." Why does the colon make the ending more dramatic?
hook.a: It makes the reader pause, then reveals the answer.

resources: Tarbiyyah Primary English scheme of work, Tomorrow's World: Develop (thriller writing; grammar: semi-colons and colons)
Punctuation Intervention Booklet (Lesson 3: Colons; Lesson 4: Semicolons) for pupils who need extra support
Display: punctuation for effect poster
Mini-whiteboard and pen
Exercise book

head: Job
Example
rows: She packed three things: a torch, a map and a code.
He froze: the door was open.
Only one person knew the password: Mia.

model.problem: Join: The corridor was silent. Something was wrong.
steps: Check: both are main clauses (they make sense alone)
Check: the ideas are closely linked
Replace the full stop with a semi-colon
Lower case after it
model.answer: The corridor was silent; something was wrong.

misconception.right: She ran to the door; it was locked. (both sides must be main clauses)

check.q: Which uses a semi-colon correctly?
options: The screen went black; the room was silent.
check.why: A joins two main clauses that are closely related.

practice.q: Add a colon for a reveal: There was only one way out the air vent.
practice.a: There was only one way out: the air vent.
practice.model: I do: the first part sets up the question (which way out?), the colon pauses, then reveals: the air vent.

practice.q: Join with a semi-colon: The alarm stopped. The silence was worse.
practice.a: The alarm stopped; the silence was worse.

practice.q: Add a colon for a list: She checked her kit a torch, a watch and a card.
practice.a: She checked her kit: a torch, a watch and a card.

independent.q: Core: write a thriller paragraph of six sentences with two colons (one list, one reveal) and two semi-colons
independent.a: A paragraph using colons and semi-colons correctly
independent.model: Labelled model: Colon (list): Mia had three minutes, one torch and a single chance. | Semi-colon: The door was locked; the vent was not. | Colon (reveal): Then she saw what was blinking on the screen: her own name.

independent.q: Extend: label each colon and semi-colon with its job
Stretch: explain why a semi-colon can be better than "and" for tension
independent.a: It creates a sharper pause and balances the two ideas, so the second hits harder.

exit.a: A) a list or a reveal

exit.q: Write one sentence with a semi-colon

lessons.homework: Write four sentences about a mystery at home: two with colons and two with semi-colons. Read for 20 minutes a day.
lessons.send: SEND: sentence halves to join with a semi-colon; colon cards. EAL: model sentences to adapt. Stretch: use a colon and a semi-colon in the same sentence correctly.

lessons.title: Brackets, dashes and hyphens: adding information and drama
lessons.bigQuestion: When should extra information be a whisper, and when should it be a shout?
objectives: To understand how brackets, dashes and hyphens add information or avoid ambiguity
successCriteria: All: use brackets for a quiet aside
Most: use dashes for dramatic parenthesis
Some: use a hyphen to avoid ambiguity in compound words

keywords.def: extra information in brackets, dashes or commas
a mark - used for drama or a pause
a short mark joining words: man-eating, re-cover
when something could mean two things

hook.text: "A man eating shark" and "a man-eating shark". What is the difference? Which would you rather meet?
hook.a: Without the hyphen it could be a man eating a shark; the hyphen shows the shark eats people.

resources: Tarbiyyah Primary English scheme of work, Tomorrow's World: Develop (thriller writing; punctuation)
Punctuation Intervention Booklet (Lesson 6: Brackets, dashes, hyphens and ellipses) for pupils who need extra support
Display: punctuation for effect poster
Mini-whiteboard and pen
Exercise book

options: There was one clue: a footprint.
There was: one clue a footprint.
starter.a: A) There was one clue: a footprint.

starter.q: Join with a semi-colon: It was late. She kept going.
starter.a: It was late; she kept going.
Extra information in brackets, dashes or commas

left.title: Brackets: quiet aside
points: The server room (on the lowest floor) was cold.

right.title: Dashes: drama
points: The server room - the one place she had been told never to go - was open.

model.problem: Add the detail "who had trained for this moment" to: Mia stepped into the dark.
steps: Is it quiet or dramatic? dramatic
Choose dashes
Place them after Mia
Check: the sentence still works without it
model.answer: Mia - who had trained for this moment - stepped into the dark.

check.q: Which phrase means a monster that eats people?
check.why: The hyphen joins man-eating into one describing word.

practice.q: Add brackets: The code was hidden in the clock. (behind the battery)
practice.a: The code was hidden in the clock (behind the battery).
practice.model: I do: the location is a quiet extra detail, so brackets, placed at the end next to clock.

practice.q: Add dashes for drama: The key was gone. (the only key)
practice.a: The key - the only key - was gone.

practice.q: Add a hyphen: a well known hacker
practice.a: a well-known hacker

independent.q: Core: improve six thriller sentences by adding brackets (two), dashes (two) and hyphens (two)
independent.model: Teacher does the first: The guard walked past. → The guard (yawning, half asleep) walked past.

independent.q: Extend: explain the effect of brackets versus dashes in one of your sentences
Stretch: write a short paragraph using a colon, a semi-colon and a dash

exit.a: B) join words and avoid ambiguity

lessons.homework: Find three hyphenated words in your reading book and write what each means. Read for 20 minutes a day.
lessons.send: SEND: parenthesis cards to slot into sentences. EAL: hyphen pairs with pictures. Stretch: write a sentence where a missing hyphen changes the meaning and explain it.

lessons.title: Bridge reading: retrieval and structure in The Lighthouse (VIPERS)
lessons.bigQuestion: How do I find exactly what a question asks for, quickly and accurately?
objectives: To retrieve and record precise information from a narrative text
successCriteria: All: find and copy short answers using key words
Most: number paragraphs and use them to locate answers
Some: answer two-mark questions with a point and evidence
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography and history: lighthouses and safety at sea
lessons.smsc: Moral: responsibility and duty (amanah, أَمَانَة): Maryam keeps the light burning to keep others safe

islamicLink.text: Responsibility and duty (amanah, أَمَانَة): Maryam keeps the light burning to keep others safe

keywords.def: find and copy information from a text
look quickly for a key word
a group of sentences about one idea
words from the text that support an answer

hook.text: A lighthouse keeper must keep the lamp lit all night in a storm. Why does one small light matter so much to a ship far out at sea?
hook.a: It shows where the dangerous rocks are, so the ship can steer away.

pictures.find: lighthouse in a storm at night photograph

starter.q: Add commas: The keeper who was tired kept watch.
starter.a: The keeper, who was tired, kept watch.
Find and copy information from a text

teach.heading: Read the text
teach.note: Read The Lighthouse aloud: Maryam keeps the lamp burning while her father mends the gallery rail in a storm; at eleven she sees a ship and signals with a lantern; the ship turns away from the rocks.

model.problem: What time did the clock chime?
steps: Underline the key word: time, clock
Which paragraph? 3
Scan for a number or time word
Copy only what is needed: eleven
model.answer: eleven

teach.heading: Two-mark answers
teach.note: Model: Why did her father go outside? He went to mend the broken rail on the gallery ("to mend the broken rail").

check.q: How many times did Maryam swing the lantern?
check.why: Paragraph 3: she swung it three times. Eleven is the time the clock chimed: a distractor.

practice.q: R: How many nights had the storm lasted?
practice.a: Three (it was the third night)
practice.model: Teacher works this one aloud: read the question, underline the key words, link it to today's rule, then give the answer in a full sentence: Three (it was the third night)

practice.q: R: What colour was the light on the water?
practice.a: yellow

independent.q: Core: answer eight retrieval questions on The Lighthouse (in the portal response box, with the sentence starter and paragraph frame)
independent.model: Teacher does the first part aloud before pupils start, showing each step: Answers copied accurately

independent.q: Extend: answer two 2-mark questions with point and evidence
Stretch: write two retrieval questions with a plausible distractor for a partner

exit.q: First step for any retrieval question?

lessons.homework: Write three retrieval questions about a page of your reading book, with answers. Read for 20 minutes a day.
lessons.send: SEND: questions name the paragraph. EAL: glossary (gallery, wick, lantern). Stretch: time yourself: eight questions in eight minutes.

lessons.title: Bridge reading: inference with evidence in The Lighthouse (VIPERS)
lessons.bigQuestion: How do I prove an inference with evidence from the text?
objectives: To make inferences about characters' feelings and motives and justify them with evidence
successCriteria: All: make an inference about Maryam's feelings
Most: support inferences with a short quotation
Some: explain how the quotation proves the inference (PEE)
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: courage and responsibility
lessons.smsc: Moral: courage and responsibility in keeping others safe

keywords.def: a conclusion from clues in the text
words copied exactly from the text, in inverted commas
give reasons and evidence
Point, Evidence, Explain

hook.text: Maryam's hands trembled, but she did not let the flame flicker. What two different things does that tell us about her?
hook.a: She was frightened, yet determined and responsible.

pictures.find: ship lights at sea at night photograph
pictures.alt: a ship's light far out at sea

starter.q: R: What was Maryam's father mending?
starter.a: the broken rail on the gallery

starter.q: Make passive: Maryam lit the lamp.
starter.a: The lamp was lit by Maryam.

head: Clue (quotation)
Inference
rows: "just as her father had taught her"
she trusts and respects her father

model.problem: How does Maryam feel when she sees the ship?
steps: Point: Maryam feels anxious but determined.
Evidence: Her hands "trembled", yet she "did not let the flame flicker".
Explain: Trembling shows fear, but keeping the flame steady shows she controls her fear to do her duty.
model.answer: A full PEE answer.

teach.heading: Avoid inventing
teach.note: Inferences must come from the text.

misconception.wrong: Maryam is angry with her father.
misconception.right: Maryam trusts her father: she signals "just as her father had taught her".

check.q: Best evidence that the ship understood the warning?
options: "began to creep away from the jagged rocks"
check.why: B shows the ship changing course after the signal.

practice.q: I: How does Maryam feel at the end? Give evidence.
practice.a: Relieved: she "let out a long, shaky breath and smiled".
practice.model: Teacher works this one aloud: read the question, underline the key words, link it to today's rule, then give the answer in a full sentence: Relieved: she "let out a long, shaky breath and smiled".

independent.q: Core: answer four inference questions using PEE (in the portal response box, with the sentence starter and paragraph frame)
independent.model: Teacher does the first part aloud before pupils start, showing each step: PEE answers

independent.q: Extend: infer the father's character with two pieces of evidence
independent.a: For example: dedicated: he had not slept since the storm began

independent.q: Stretch: reading journal: Explain how the writer builds tension in paragraph 3
independent.a: Short sentences, a ticking clock, the tiny light

lessons.homework: Reading journal: Zoom in on a character in your book and make one inference with evidence. Read for 20 minutes a day.
lessons.send: SEND: PEE frame with sentence starters. EAL: feelings word bank. Stretch: compare Maryam's feelings at the start and end.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Reading skills for the SATs - The Lighthouse
lessons.title: Vocabulary in context and the effect of language
objectives: Explain the meaning of words and phrases in context
Explain how language choices affect the reader

keywords.def: surrounding words that help show meaning
a comparison using like or as
the feeling a word suggests
the impression made on the reader

starter: Bismillah. Make an inference: Her hands trembled.
Predict: The storm was getting worse.
Find and copy: the colour of the light on the water.

teach.heading: Meaning in context
bullets: Look at words around the word
Replace it with your own word
Check the sentence still makes sense
teach.note: Model: 'the sea heaved' - find a similar word: rose and fell with great force. Do not just give a dictionary definition if the question says 'in this context'.

teach.heading: Key words from the text
teach.note: Pupils choose the best meaning from options. Explain how to eliminate wrong choices. Use another word with the same meaning and test in the sentence.

teach.heading: Similes and effect
bullets: like a wild animal trapped in a cage
Explain: the sea wants to escape and is dangerous
teach.note: Break down the comparison: wild animal = fierce, unpredictable; cage = trapped, struggling. Teach the structure: technique, quotation, effect on the reader.

teach.heading: Word choice
bullets: heaved and roared: the sea sounds alive
teach.note: Ask pupils how the sea 'roared' is different from 'moved'. Discuss how verbs give the sea personality. Link to personification.

teach.heading: Write an effect answer
teach.note: Provide a model: 'The word "roared" makes the sea sound like an angry animal, which makes the reader feel the danger.' Pupils write their own.

practice: What does the word 'jagged' suggest about the rocks?
What impression does the phrase 'trapped in a cage' give of the sea?
Find and copy a word that shows how slowly the ship turned.
independent: Answer eight vocabulary and language questions.
Explain the effect of two phrases in full sentences.
Write a simile of your own to describe a storm.
exit: What does 'bobbed' suggest about the light?
Complete: The simile suggests the sea is...
lessons.homework: Choose two vivid phrases from a book and explain their effect.
lessons.send: SEND: vocabulary cards with images. EAL: pre-teach key verbs. Stretch: compare how the sea and Maryam are presented.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Reading skills for the SATs - The Lighthouse
lessons.title: Summarising, structure and comparison
objectives: Summarise a paragraph or section
Explain how the order of ideas affects meaning

keywords.def: give the main points briefly
how a text is organised
say how two things are similar or different
a group of sentences about one idea

starter: Bismillah. Explain the effect of the word 'roared'.
Find and copy: what Maryam used to signal.

teach.heading: Summarising
teach.note: Model summarising paragraph 3: Maryam keeps the lamp burning and spots a ship, which she signals. Explain that a summary is short. SAT questions often ask for a short summary of what a paragraph is about.

teach.heading: Match summaries
bullets: Choose the best title for each paragraph
Para 3: the signal; para 4: the ship turns
teach.note: Ask pupils to match headings to paragraphs. Include a wrong heading and discuss why it does not fit. Link to answering 'Which of these best summarises...?'

teach.heading: Structure
teach.note: Ask why the author describes the sea first. It sets the mood and danger. Explain how the order of ideas builds tension: setting, instruction, action, outcome.

teach.heading: Comparing
bullets: Compare Maryam at the start and end
End: smiled, let out a breath
teach.note: Teach comparative language. Write one sentence comparing the beginning and end. Ask for evidence. Also compare Maryam and her father.

teach.heading: Write a comparison answer
teach.note: Model: 'At the start, Maryam is anxious because she presses her nose against the glass; at the end, she smiles, which shows relief.' Pupils produce their own.

practice: Which is the best title for paragraph 2?
Why does the author begin with a description of the sea?
How is Maryam different at the end of the extract?
independent: Write a one-sentence summary of each paragraph.
Answer four structure and comparison questions.
Compare Maryam and her father in a short paragraph.
lessons.homework: Summarise a chapter of a book you are reading in three sentences.
lessons.send: SEND: matching headings to paragraphs. EAL: provide comparison sentence starters. Stretch: explain what would change if the story began with the signal.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Reading skills for the SATs - The Lighthouse
lessons.title: Timed reading practice and review
objectives: Apply reading skills to a new text under timed conditions
Review answers and set targets

keywords.def: planning how long to spend on each section
a skill to improve next
guidance showing what earns marks
look back and improve

starter: Bismillah. Name the eight reading skills (vocabulary, retrieval, ...).
What should you do first when reading a text?
How can you check an inference answer?

teach.heading: Plan your time
teach.note: Explain the pacing plan. In the real test pupils may use the whole hour; this plan helps. Model starting with easy questions.

teach.heading: Question types
teach.note: Show how each question type is answered. Provide a quick example for each from The Lighthouse. Remind them to read instructions carefully.

teach.heading: Mark scheme thinking
bullets: 2 marks need two points or point + evidence
Accept different wording if the meaning is right
teach.note: Share simplified mark scheme language. Explain that precise, relevant answers earn marks and that vague answers do not. Ask pupils to improve a weak answer.

teach.heading: Practise
teach.note: Share the unseen text (Layla's Market Stall, below) and set the questions in the independent task. Layla's Market Stall. Every Saturday, Layla helped her grandfather set up his stall in the old market square. By seven o'clock, the air smelled of cinnamon and fresh bread. Her grandfather arranged the dates in neat pyramids while Layla polished the brass scales until they gleamed. 'Customers buy with their eyes first,' he told her, smiling. By midday, a long queue snaked around the fountain. Layla weighed, wrapped and counted change as quickly as she could, though her arms ached. When the last customer had gone, her grandfather pressed a small bag of dates into her hands. 'For the best assistant in the market,' he said. Layla grinned: she had never felt so proud. Monitor timing. Encourage calm. Say a short dua before starting if desired.

teach.heading: Review and set targets
teach.note: Go through answers. Ask pupils to identify the kind of question they missed. Write a target such as 'use a quotation in inference answers'.

practice: Order these steps: answer, read, check.
